insider_note: This equation's final integral splits into a 1/v² term and a 1/v term, not one clean log — write both antiderivatives separately (−1/v and −3 log v) before combining, rather than trying to force one combined log form too early.

steps.label: Recognise homogeneous form and substitute
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Every term on both sides has total degree 3 in x and y, so the equation is homogeneous.
steps.memory_tip: Check the degree of EVERY term, not just one — x²y, xy², x³ and x²y are all degree 3.
lines: Every term top and bottom has degree 3, so
steps.why: Every term of both the numerator and denominator has total degree 3 in x and y, so dividing every term by x³ after substituting y = vx leaves a function of v alone, confirming the homogeneous form.
common_mistakes: Missing a factor of x when expanding (vx)² = v²x², undercounting the degree.
Dividing numerator and denominator by different powers of x by mistake.

steps.label: Separate the variables
steps.margin_note: One mark. Subtract v as a fraction with denominator (1 − 3v) before combining.
steps.memory_tip: v(1 − 3v) = v − 3v² is the piece that cancels part of the numerator, leaving v² behind.

lines.text: Take v to the right side:

steps.why: Writing v as v(1 − 3v)/(1 − 3v) puts both terms over the same denominator, and expanding v − 2v² − v + 3v² leaves exactly v², which is what makes the equation separable.
common_mistakes: Losing the −v term when expanding v(1 − 3v) = v − 3v².
Sign error turning v² into −v² in the final numerator.

steps.label: Integrate both sides
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Split (1 − 3v)/v² into 1/v² − 3/v before integrating each piece separately.
steps.memory_tip: 1/v² integrates to −1/v; 1/v integrates to log v — two different rules, so split first.
steps.why: The fraction (1 − 3v)/v² splits into two separate standard integrals, ∫v⁻²dv = −1/v and −3∫(1/v)dv = −3 log v, which together match the right side's ∫dx/x = log x.
common_mistakes: Integrating 1/v² as log v² instead of −1/v.
Losing the factor of 3 in front of log v.

steps.label: Return to x and y
steps.margin_note: One mark. Combine log x + 3 log v + log c into a single log before substituting v = y/x.
steps.memory_tip: 3 log v = log v³, so the whole right side is log(cxv³).

lines.text: Collect the logs on one side:
3 log v = log v³, and the logs combine:

steps.why: Combining all the log terms into log(cxv³) before substituting keeps the working compact, and replacing v by y/x turns the whole relation back into the original variables.
common_mistakes: Substituting v = y/x before combining the logs, leading to a fraction inside a fraction.
Writing x/v³ instead of xv³ when combining the log terms.

steps.label: Final equation
steps.margin_note: The last mark. Remove the log by exponentiating both sides, then isolate c.
steps.memory_tip: log A = B means A = e to the power B — apply that once to remove the log entirely.

lines.text: log A = B means A = e to the power B:

steps.why: Exponentiating both sides of log(cy³/x²) = −x/y removes the log, and rearranging for c gives the family of solutions in the exact form the book marks — the relation between x, y and the arbitrary constant.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to exponentiate BOTH sides, leaving a log on one side only.
Inverting the fraction and writing c = (y³/x²)·e to the power (−x/y) instead of (x²/y³)·e to the power (−x/y).
